Death of Hon. John W. Smith. Rock Port, Mo., Aug. 28.—(Special.) Hon. John W. Smith died at his home here this morning, after an illness of nearly two years. Mr. Smith was for about fourteen years clerk of the circuit court of Atchison county and represented the county in the Missouri legislature for one term. He was a member of North Star lodge, No. 157, A. F. and A. M., Zerubabel chapter, No. 59, and Rock Port lodge, No. 125, I. O. O. F. He was a member of the Methodst Episcopal church. The funeral will be held under charge of the Masons next Sunday morning. TELEGRAPHIC BRIEFS.
Athens, Ga., Aug. 28.—William Haygood, while profaning on Monday at the High shoals, declaring there was no God, no heaven and no hell, had his tongue paralyzed. The matter has caused a great sensation in that community.

Ajaccio, Corsica, Aug. 28.—A duel with pistols was fought near here to-day between Senor Beneditti, a journalist, and Dr. Alessandri. The latter was killed. The quarrel which brought about the encounter grew out of a political discussion.

Ivrea, Italy, Aug. 28.—It now appears that fourteen persons were killed and a number were injured by the fire which broke out in the church at Ribordone, caused by the explosion of a lamp and which spread to the pilgrim shelter, adjoining the church, where most of the persons were burned to death.

Excelsior Springs, Mo., Aug. 28.—(Special.) Last night someone went to the city jail here and took out a colored man and a white man, who had confessed to a nameless crime. They were taken about a mile from the city and the colored man was stripped and severely whipped. The white man begged off and the two were allowed to go free.

Grasshoppers Doomed. TOPEKA, Kan., Aug. 29.—The grasshopper problem has been solved. W. H. Hossack of Great Bend is the inventor of a "hopper mill" which means death to the pests. It is a header with a screen at the back and wings of canvas at the ends and canvas cover. When the machine starts the hoppers fly into it and drop on the slatted canvas that is used for elevating the grain and are carried swiftly between two rollers and are ground up. Ecuador's Revolutionists Win.
GUAYAQUIL, Ecuador, Aug. 29.—The war in Ecuador is virtually ended, Quito having pronounced in favor of General Alfaro. Belisario Alban Mertana has been appointed temporarily military and civil chief of the city. The forces of the Conservative government fled in disorder at the approach of the patriots. The first act of these on their assumption of government was to liberate all political prisoners.

Shot Dead in His Office.

PITTSBURG, Pa., Aug. 29.—James Getty, an ex-councilman and a wealthy wholesale liquor dealer, was shot and killed in his office this morning by Alexander Hutchinson, formerly proprietor of the Merchants hotel in this city. Getty was the owner of the Hotel Willey, and the murder was the result of a dispute over the leasing of the hotel to Hutchinson.

May Be Pulled Off at Juarez.

DENVER, Col., Aug. 29.—A special to the Times from Elapso says: It is understood that matters have been fixed at Mexico city with the federal officials so that the Corbett-Fitzsimmons fight can be pulled off in Juarez, but has been held back by President Diaz heretofore. Twenty-thousand dollars Mexican money must be put up as a guarantee for local expenses and evidence of good faith.

Reported Against Supt. Swett.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 29.—Three special agents of the Indian office have reported against J. A. Swett, superintendent of the Haskell institute at Lawrence, Kan. They insist in the reports made that he should be removed from the position he now holds owing to his inability to fill it creditably.

Hogs Mutilate a Body.

SOUTH McALESTER, I. T., Aug. 29.—An unknown man was found dead near this place yesterday. When found the hogs had mutilated his body so as to be unrecognizable. No marks of violence were found on his person except that his left arm was broken. His remains were buried here to-day.

Whipped by Whitecaps.

EXCELSIOR SPRINGS, Mo., Aug. 29.—Last night masked men took out of the jail here a negro and an Irishman charged with viciousness and whipped them with cowhides.
excelsior-springs-excelsior-springs-1895.A3:
A Windfall for a Bank. PAINESVILLE, Ohio, Aug. 31.—When the Painesville Savings bank collapsed four years ago among the assets found was $250,000 worth of stock in a Western mine. At that time the mine was thought to be worthless, but it is paying a fair dividend, and the stock is nearly at par. The indications are that the depositors in the wrecked bank will secure a good dividend, with the prospects that ultimately they may receive their deposits back in full. Salvation Army Cavalry.
DENVER, Col., Aug. 31.—The Salvation army of Denver organized a cavalry corps of young women yesterday and last night Brigadier General French of St. Louis dedicated the new branch of the service at the First Baptist church, which was hardly large enough to accommodate the crowd. This corps enjoys the distinction of being the only mounted Salvation army fighters in the world.

The Wrong Man Was Killed.

GRAND RAPIDS, Mich., Aug. 31.—John Smalley, the supposed train robber, killed by deputy sheriffs at McBain, was, it has been learned, at Brinton visiting his old neighbors last week at the time of the hold-up and until after the killing of Detective Powers in this city. The train robbers and the murderer of Detective Powers are still at large and the officers have as yet obtained no definite clue as to their identity.

White Caps to be Prosecuted.

EXCELSIOR SPRINGS, Mo., Aug. 31. Nothing has been heard from the two men who were taken from the city jail here and whipped Tuesday night. The colored people are highly incensed and have taken steps to have it legally investigated.

CONDENSED DISPATCHES.

The steamer Bawnmore, ashore in Oregon, is a total loss.

Rain deluged the Johnson county, Kan., fair exhibits at Olathe.

The Kentucky Democratic state committee issued an address to the party, pleading for harmony.

It is said that the administration is going to turn down General Miles in selecting a successor to General Schofield.

Four prisoners escaped from the Stoddard county, Missouri, jail by sawing the bars in two.

BLACKSAND WHITES FIGHT
A Pitched Battle in Georgia Between
Two Armed Factions.
ATLANTA Ga Aug. 2 — A pitched bet-
ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 2.—A pitched battle between Marietta and Atlanta took place about two miles east in Cobb county. The opposing forces were a posse of white men on one side, searching for a negro assaulter, and on the other side five or six negroes. Friends and relatives of the woman were on foot and armed with Winchester, rifles and shotguns, while the negroes were in wagons and on mules, all fully armed.

Saturday night last Jesse Hardeman, a negro farm hand 25 years of age, attempted to assault in a most brutal manner the wife of J. H. Robinson, who lives two miles from Marietta. The cries of the woman brought her husband to the house but before she could acquaint him with the negro's purpose, he had escaped.

A posse was immediately organized and a search of the surrounding country began. About twenty men were out searching for him last night, when they met a party of negroes on the road. Suddenly one of the negroes arose in the wagon and leveling a double-barreled shotgun at the approaching party, fired both barrels. Charles Boughly received ninety buckshot in the left arm.

The white men returned the fire until some hundred shots had been exhausted. A mule on which one of the negroes was mounted fell, but the rider and his companions fled. This morning a hat worn by one of the negroes was discovered by the road side saturated with blood.

None of the negroes have been found, although Sheriff Davenport of Cobb county has organized a very large posse and is today scouring the surrounding country for the negroes, and a great uprising of the negroes is imminent. Nearly every white and colored man is armed and they are moving about the road this afternoon in an ominous and threatening manner.
jesse-hardeman-marietta-1895-07-27.A4:
A BATTLE WITH A POSSE.
Four Negroes and a White Man Seriously Wounded.
Atlanta, Ga., Aug. 2.—A posse, which was out last night hunting for Jesse Hardeman, a negro, met his father, a brother, and some friends near Smyrna, Cobb county, and a battle followed. Hardeman's father started the shooting, and he had heard that his son had been lynched and he and some friends started for the scene. On the way the negroes met a posse of whites. Joe Hardeman fired the first shot and then an engagement began and became general. Four negroes and one white man were seriously wounded. Jesse Hardeman was not found. He is wanted for attempting to make a criminal assault on Mrs. Joseph Robinson.
jesse-hardeman-marietta-1895-07-27.A7:
A WAR OF RACES IMMINENT.
Whites and Negroes Fight a Pitched Battle in Georgia.
A Great Negro Uprising Threatened in Cobb County, Where Everybody, White and Black is Armed—The Trouble Caused by the Attempt of a Negro to Bape a White Woman.
ATLANTA, Ga., August 3.—A pitched battle between Marietta and Atlanta took place about two miles east, in Cobb county. The opposing forces were a posse of white men on one side, searching for a negro rapist and on the other side five or six negroes. Friends and relatives of the woman were on foot and armed with Winchester rifles and shot guns, while the negroes were in wagons and on mules, fully armed.

Saturday night last Jesse Hardeman, a negro farm hand, 25 years of age, attempted to assault, in a most brutal manner, the wife of J. R. Robinson, who lives two miles from Marietta. The cries of the woman brought her husband to the house, but before she could acquaint him with the negro's purpose, the fiend had escaped.

A posse was immediately organized and a search of the surrounding country for Hardeman began. About twenty men were out searching for him last night when they met a party of negroes on the road. Suddenly one of the negroes arose in the wagon and leveling a double-barrelled shot gun at the approaching party fired both barrels. Charles Dougty received ninety buckshot in his left arm.

The white men returned the fire until some hundred shots had been exchanged. A mule on which one of the negroes was mounted fell, but the rider and his companions fled. This morning a hat worn by one of the negroes was discovered by the roadside saturated with blood. None of the negroes have yet been found, although Sheriff Davenport, of Cobb county, has organized a large posse and is scouring the surrounding country for the negroes, and a great uprising of the negroes is imminent. Nearly every one, white and colored, is armed.
jesse-hardeman-marietta-1895-07-27.A9:
CLASH OF THE RACES IN COBB.
THE FOUR NEGRO PRISONERS UP IN COURT.
Two of the Accused Held for the Action of the Grand Jury—One of Them Accused of Assaulting a Woman With Intent to Murder and the Other Charged With Riot. Story of the Blacks.

Marietta, Ga., Aug. 3.—The four negroes who were arrested as a result of the riot below Smyrna night before last were all brought before Judge J. Y. Alexander for a hearing.

The court house was filled with a large crowd to witness the proceedings. Berry Padgett, who received a load of shot in the back of his head, neck and shoulders, and never stopped running afterward until he reached Marietta, waived a commitment trial, and gave bond to appear at the superior court.

John Hardeman, a negro over 50 years of age, the father of Jesse Hardeman, who assaulted Mrs. Robinson, was placed on trial for assault with intent to murder. His statement was in substance that
he and Tom Hardeman, Berry Padgett and Berry Smith had heard that Jesse Hardeman had been lynched and were on their way to Collins' bridge, over the Chattahoochee, at Bolton, to see if he had been hung there, as reported. They had got nearly to the bridge, and becoming satisfied that the report was not true, they turned back to go home.

They met three men, one of whom was Virgil Fleming. He pointed a pistol in Berry Padgett's face and another of the three pointed a pistol at John. Padgett and John were in the cart together. They told Padgett to drive up the road and give an account of themselves. The negroes did so and met a large crowd of armed white men.

Tom Hardeman and Berry Smith were riding mules. Norris Pace walked up and said: "Tom, give up your gun." Tom gave up his gun and they then said: "Throw up your hands," and as they did so the white men began shooting. John jumped out of the cart, fired and ran and received a bullet shot through the left leg.

Hardeman was held for the action of the grand jury.

Jake Thompson, another negro, was discharged.
William Hardeman was held for riot.
No more trouble is expected at Smyrna.

GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
NEWS OF THE TWO STATES TOLD IN PARAGRAPHS.
GEORGIA.

The State Agricultural association will meet at Cumberland Aug. 13, 14 and 15.

The building prospects in Tifton for the last half of 1895 is the expenditure of about $75,000.

James Bryant of Dahlonega recently killed a rattlesnake measuring three feet and ten inches and having thirteen rattles.

There will be more work in the way of new houses and additions in Cleveland than the carpenters can do from now until winter.

Fireman Hodo of the Georgia road, who was injured in the wreck at Union Point some weeks ago, has brought suit against the road for $5,000 damages.

The Macon and Indian Springs Electric Railway Company wants to extend its line to Central City Park. The Consolidated Company at present owns the only line to the park.

The dry goods store of W. W. Miller at Milledgeville was entered by burglars Monday night. About $100 in silver and some goods were stolen. No clew to the robbers has been found.

Sheriff Fisher of Colquitt county, is now corresponding with some regular dealer in Kentucky in reference to purchasing some bloodhounds for the use of the county in catching criminals.

Many farmers of Houston county say more corn will be harvested in Houston this year than in any year since the war. The acreage is more extensive, and the yield per acre will be larger than usual.

It has been ordered that, commencing this week, all conductors, firemen, engineers, and other trainmen of the Port Royal railroad will have to reside at Port Royal. Heretofore they lived in Augusta.

The Reformed Associated Presbyterians of Atlanta, who have been worshipping for some years out in Whitehall street, have bought a lot corner Lloyd and Garnett. They are preparing to build a handsome church. The work was begun Monday.

A meeting has been called in Atlanta on Aug. 15 for the purpose of organizing a Southern Traveling Passenger Agents and Passenger Agents Association. The territory will include the railroad region south of the Ohio and Potomac rivers and west of the Mississippi.

Up to date but one man in Lumpkin county has registered to make brandy this season and that is Thomas Sain of Mill Creek district. The bond is not so easy made as heretofore. It is $300 and two of the bondsmen have to be worth over and above the homestead.

Kennedy, teacher of one of the public colored schools in Elbert county, at one of the colored churches at Elberton last Sunday made an oration to quite a number of his people in which he took occasion to throw out many unbecoming expressions highly calculated to incite race feeling and to create bitterness between the whites and blacks. Commissioner James N. Wall quietly investigated the matter and found the charges true and promptly revoked Kennedy's license. Kennedy is also editor of the Elberton Progress.

Jesse Hardeman, the negro who assaulted Mrs. Robinson, at Symrna has not yet been arrested. It was reported Tuesday morning that he was being concealed at a negro's house near Gilmore station, four miles south of Symrna. A large posse of men has gone to search for him. Jake Thomas, who furnished a mule for one of the negroes to ride the night of the assault, was discharged. Tom Hardeman and Berry Padgett are held for court. Nothing of Berry Smith has been learned since his mysterious disappearance.

Tax Receiver R. L. Foster has finished making up his returns for the year and Floyd county joins those which show a slump. This is in spite of the fact that the county is prospering in the way of new industries and the organization of old ones. Many attempts are made to explain this seeming inconsistency, but nothing appears to fit the opinion of officials except a general shrinkage in valuation. The shrinkage amounts to $292,694. The valuation of the property is something over $7,500,000, a shrinkage of about $1,000,-000 in the past two years. As the population has increased and many improvements have been made and money circulated, the normal increase should have been twice the amount of the slump.

Ben Arnold, while plowing the other day near Dawson, had an experience with a rattlesnake that was anything but pleasant. While passing a cluster of bushes and a stump in the field he heard the well-known signal of this most venomous of reptiles, and stopped to make an investigation of its whereabouts. Mr. Arnold had not turned loose his plowstock when, looking down, he was horrified to find that a large rattlesnake had it rangs fastened in one of his trousers legs. He realized the danger of his situation at once, and, placing his foot on the reptile's head, soon dispatched it. It was soon afterwards discovered that the horse Mr. Arnold was plowing had been bitten by the snake. Antidotes were applied and the animal is now about well.

Cosby E. Smith committed suicide at 1 o'clock Monday afternoon by cutting his throat from ear to ear at the home of his sister, Mrs. Nall, at Newnan. Mr. Smith, who had been ill with fever in Florida, came home Monday and went to the residence of his sister. He told Mrs. Nall he was not feeling well, and went to his room in the second story of the house. Mrs. Nall sent a servant with his dinner. About 1 o'clock a crimson spot showed on the ceiling of the room under that occupied by Mr. Smith and blood began dripping to the floor. Mrs. Nall and the servants ran to the room above and found the suicide with a horrible gash in his throat which had severed his jugular vein. Beside him lay a bloody razor. Smith was already dead. No cause for the act is assigned except ill health. The suicide was 44 years old and unmarried.

Considerable building is being done at Cochran and several handsome buildings have already been completed. A fine brick building is being built by Dr. C. E. Taylor to cost $5,000. The Masonic building just finished cost between six and seven thousand dollars, and a splendid hotel cost nearly $10,000. The new brick stores are being built by Wynne and Brother and W. M. and J. N. Wynne. The dwellings belonging to Messrs. Morgan Thompson, S. Phillips, Dr. Henderson, H. Hanell and Mrs. Pace on Cherry and Sixth streets are fine additions. The residences of Mrs. A. P. Grundy, R. J. Morgan, J. M. Blackshear, J. C. Dunnam, W. M. Wynne and J. W. Jenkins, adorn the town with new and beautifying appearances, while two new dormitories at the college and an artesian well building swell the list of Cochran's improvements.

jesse-hardeman-marietta-1895-07-27.A14:
SMYRNA'S TROUBLE.
A Negro Assaults a White Woman.
IT CREATES GREAT EXCITEMENT.
Indignant Citizens in their Hunt for Him Have to Fight Some Armed Negroes.
Smyrna, in this county, was in a fever of excitement last week. It was the result of a criminal assault made upon Mr. Joe Robinson's wife by a negro named Jesse Hardeman, on Tuesday evening of last week. Mr. Robinson and Hardeman are tenants on Mr. Polly Baswell's farm.

Hardeman went to Mr. Robinson's house to carry in some wood, having left Mr. Robinson in the field with other hands, who in quitting the day's work were indulging in eating some watermelons.

The negro Hardeman in finding Mrs. Robinson alone with her young baby, seized hold of her. She struggled and got away from the negro and grabbed her husband's pistol, and scared him off by pointing it at him. She didn't know how to shoot the pistol, and the negro attempted the second time to assault her. She used the pistol to scare him again and closed the doors and called for her husband. The negro got Mr. Baswell's cow and was driving her on up the road, when the husband came to the house and was informed of the matter. He took his pistol and started in pursuit. Hardeman saw him coming and broke for the woods and made his escape.

The neighbors turned out to hunt for the fugitive with their guns and pistols, that night. On the public highway, near Mr. King's house, they met four negro men, two in a cart and two on mules. The negroes were armed with guns and so were the whites. The negroes were John Hardeman, the father of the fugitive, Tom Hardeman, a brother, Berry Pedgett and Berry Smith. It is said the negroes were bent on preventing the lynching of Jesse Hardeman, and they were returning from Bolton, having heard that he had been hung to the river bridge.

When tae whites met the negroes they demanded them to give an account of themselves and to surrender their guns. Words passed, and John Hardeman, colored, jumped out of his cart and fired at Charley Dowda, filling his left hand with shot. Then a fusilade began and the negroes fled. The result was, John Hardeman was shot with a bullet in the leg, Tom received a bullet in his leg. Berry Padgett was shot in the back of his head and shoulders with bird shot, and Berry Smith has never been seen since. It is not known whether he was killed or wounded. Two mules were badly shot, one died.

Mr. Charlie Dowda had sixty-five shot picked out of his hand.

On Saturday the three negroes had their preliminary trial before Judge J. Y. Alexander at the Marietta court house, Padgett was represented by Hon. A. S. Clay and waived trial and gave bond for his appearance before Cobb Superior Court. John and Tom Hardeman were represented by Hon. John E. Mozley. Col. C. D. Phillips and E. P. Green, Esq., represented the State.

John Hardeman at the trial made the following statement:

"He and Tom Hardeman, Berry Padgett and Berry Smith had heard that Jesse Hardeman had been lynched and were on their way to Collin's bridge, over the Chattahoochee, at Bolton, to see if he had been hung there as reported. They got nearly to the bridge, and becoming satisfied that the report was not true, they turned back to go home. They met three men, one of whom was Virgil Fleming. He pointed a pistol in Berry Padgett's face and another of the three pointed a pistol at John. Padgett and John were in the cart together. They told Padgett to drive on up the road and give an account of themselves. The negroes did so and met a large crowd of white men. Tom Hardeman and Berry Smith were riding mules. Norris Pace walked up and said, "Tom, give up your gun." Tom gave up his gun and they then said, "Throw up your hands," and as they did so the white men began shooting. John jumped out of the cart, fired and ran and received a bullett shot through his left leg.

Berry Padgett testified: "When we got in the crowd they asked us to stop and we stopped. They then asked us our business, and where we were going, and so forth, and some young man with a pistol in his hand came up and continued to talk with John Hardeman. About this time John jumped out of the cart and as he did so struck my mule with his gun and he ran twenty or thirty yards while I was trying to check him. About that time somebody poured a load of shot into my neck, head and shoulders. I thought it a

When Mr. Pace said 'Give up your guns' I told the others to do so. I had no gun myself."

Tom Hardeman corroberated his father. Tom said that when they passed Charley Dowda and Virgil Fleming and another man down the road, the whites followed them till the main crowd in the rear of these three was reached. "Dowda shot first and then I jumped off my mule and began running. I received a bullet hole through my leg."

John Hardeman was ten or twenty feet from Dowda and I was about ten feet from him.

"The negroes had three guns; two muzzle loaders and one breech loader. There were twenty or thirty in our crowd. I saw somebody holding one end of Tom's gun while Tom was holding to the other end. This was after the shooting began and after John Hardeman had jumped out of the cart."

Virgil Fleming testifies as follows: John Hardeman jumped out of the cart and shot at Charley Dowda twice and said to the negroes with him, 'Shoot, boys.' I had a pistol in my hand at that time, but did not point it in anybody's face. The crowd was armed with all sorts of weapons. The negroes, Tom Hardeman, Jesse Hardeman and Berry Smith, had guns. I was along because I had been deputized to hunt for Jesse Hardeman."

After speeches from counsel the defendant was committed for assault with intent to murder in default of a $500 bond.

William Hardeman and John Hardeman were placed on trial charged with riot. It resulted in their commitment on the charge, and the bond against Tom was placed at $200.

On this hearing Bob Fleming testified to a very narrow escape from death on the part of Mr. Norris Pace, one of Smyrna's best citizens. He says that when Pace walked up to the negroes Tom Hardeman leveled his gun at Pace's breast and snapped, bursting the cap, but not causing the gun to fire. This alone saved his life. The gun, when finally secured corroborated this statement.

Virgil Fleming swore that he saw John Hardeman shoot twice at Dowda and Berry Smith shot at Fleming. He saw the flash of the pistol and judged from that.

On this trial John Hardeman admitted that he shot once and then ran, but said it was after the crowd began firing.

The warrant against Jacob Thomas was dismissed, as there was no case against him. He had only allowed one of the parties to ride his mule without knowing their purpose, and was regarded as an old and inoffensive darky. He was represented by Mr. George D. Anderson.

The excitement was so high at one time Friday night, that the Marietta Rifles were notified to hold themselves in readiness to go to Smyrna, but they were not needed as the matter was unduly magnified. Everything is serene now.

Lee Kincer Acquitted. SERGENT, Ky., Aug. 9.—Lee Kincer, the slayer of Spencer Adams, a young teacher of this county, on Pine creek, in August, 1894, was tried before Judge Blair at Whitesburg Thursday and acquitted. It seems that the two men were playing with an old pistol in Kincer's hands, when it discharged and killed young Adams. It lately developed that Kincer used some ugly language to Adams on the day of the killing. Correspondents Not Forgotten.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., Aug. 9.—In the plans for the entertainment of visitors during the G. A. R. encampment, the many special newspaper correspondents are not overlooked. They will be extended the hospitalities of the city, and the members of the local press have arranged to provide everything for their comfort and convenience.

Jail Delivery at Leitchfield.

LEITCHFIELD, Ky., Aug. 9.—Bird Skaggs and Tim Salsman escaped from the county jail here. They were held for larceny. They escaped by cutting a hole in the brick wall, and lowered themselves to the ground by means of blankets tied together.

A Lynching Expected.

LEBANON, Ky., Aug. 9.--Sheriff Simms, of Washington county, left here Thursday night with Matthew Lewis, the Negro charged with assault upon Mrs. Murray, this week. It is said his arrival in Washington county will be followed by a lynching.

Ex-Treasurer Riggle's Shortage.

LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 9.—Ex-Treasurer Riggle, of Pendleton county, has been found nearly $9,000 short in his accounts and the fiscal court has appointed a committee to settle the matter by arbitration. If this fails the court will bring suit.

New Kentucky Pensioners.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 9.—Pensions were issued as follows: Increase, Stephen H. Hicks, Cove Dale, Lewis county. Original widow, etc., Margaret Studier, Newport; minor of Joseph C. Bourland, Marion. Crittenden.
matthew-lewis-springfield-1895-08-12.A2:
LYNCHING AVERTED.
Mob Was Too Full to Carry Out Their Intentions.
LEBANON Ky., Aug. 11.—A mob of about forty men went to the Springfield jail about 1 o'clock this morning, and demanded of the jailor the keys leading to the cells of Matthew Lewis and Jesse Ray, who assaulted Mrs. Shields recently. The jailor, seeing resistance was useless, handed over the keys, and the mob at once proceeded to business Everybody in the mob was drunk, and none of them seemed to be able to unlock the jail door. After working about the locks and bolts without result, they secured sledge hammers, and tried to break down the doors They proved too strong for them, however, and after two hours' hard work, they abandoned the job. They then emptied their revolvers into the cells of the jail, but no one was hit. Returning the keys to the jailor, they told him they would be back tonight and left town. The mob was composed of men from Washington and Marion counties. The two negroes will be confined at Louisville until the excitement at Springfield is over.
matthew-lewis-springfield-1895-08-12.A11:
MOB WAS TOO DRUNK
TOOK TOO MUCH WHISKY TO DO
THEIR WORK.
Two Negroes Escape from the Hands of a Savage Mob Organized to Lynch Them.
Louisville, Ky., August 12.—A special to the Commercial from Lebanon, Ky., says:

A mob of about forty men went to the Springfield jail about 1 o'clock yesterday morning and demanded of the jailer the keys leading to the cells of Matthew Lewis and Jesse Ray, who outraged Mrs. Shields, white, recently. The jailer seeing that resistance was useless, handed over the keys and the mob at once proceeded to business.

As everybody in the mob was drunk none of them seemed able to unlock the jail doors. After working at the locks and bolts without success they procured sledge hammers and tried to batter down the doors. The doors proved too strong for them, however, and after two hours of hard work they abandoned the job.

They then emptied their revolvers into the cells of the jail, but no one was hit. Returning the keys to the jailer they told him they would be back again tonight and left town. The mob was composed of men from Washington and Marion counties, nine of them, it is said, being from this city.

The sheriff of Washington county passed through this city today with Lewis and Ray on their way to Louisville, where the two negroes will be confined until the excitement at Springfield is over.

Louisville, Ky., August 12.—Sheriff Craycroft of Washington county arrived here last night with Lewis and Ray, the negroes who came so near being lynched at Springfield early yesterday morning. The prisoners were placed in the county jail and will be kept there for the present. The prisoners had a close call for their lives. Had they remained at Springfield tonight they would surely have been lynched.

matthew-lewis-springfield-1895-08-12.A13:
THE MOB BAFFLED.
They Tried to Unlock the Springfield, Ky., Jail, But Failed.

LEBANON, Ky., Aug. 13.—A mob of 40 men went to Springfield, a village nine miles north of this city. Sunday morning, for the purpose of hanging Matthew Lewis and Jesse Ray, Negroes confined in the jail there charged with criminal assault on Mrs. Murray Shields, a white woman, last Monday morning. The mob took the jailer by surprise, and he, seeing that resistance was useless, handed over the keys.

After trying to work the locks and failing, they procured hammers and tried to break the doors down, but in this they also failed. The mob then marched around the jail, shooting into the windows, hoping in this way to kill the negroes, but none of their shots took effect. They then dispersed, threatening to return.

FOUR MURDERERERS LYNCHED.
Short Work of a California Mob This Morning.
Short Work of a California Mob This Morning.

YREKA, Cal., August 26.—Four murderers confined in the county jail here—Johnson, Semlock, Null and Moreno—were taken from jail by a mob at 2 o'clock this morning and hanged in the jail yard.

Lynching of a Colored Man Presumably by Colored Men.

SPRINGFIELD, Ky., August 26.—Shortly after 2 o'clock this morning a mob composed of about a dozen men took Harrison Lewis, the negro who murdered Joe Brooks, also colored, last Friday night, from the jail here, and hanged him to a tree in the court house yard. When the mob reached the jail they called for Jailer Smith, but his wife informed them that he was not at home, and that he had the keys to the jail with him.

This did not daunt the mob, however. Going to a blacksmith shop near by, they procured some sledge hammers, and after three hours' work succeeded in battering down the jail door. Lewis was found crouching in his cell, and begged piteously for his life, but the leader ordered the men to make quick work of him. He was quickly seized, and after placing a rope around his neck was dragged to the nearest tree and strung up without further ceremony.

The mob did its work in a quiet, orderly way, and seemed to be thoroughly organized. It is the opinion of many that it was composed of colored men. After completing their work the mob quietly dispersed.

The murder was a dastardly one, and the regrces have been greatly worked up since its occurrence. Friday night Lewis went to Brooks' house, and, calling him to the door, shot him down on his own threshold, without any warning.

Harrison Lewis, the man who was lynched, was a brother of Matthew Lewis, who narrowly escaped lynching here about two weeks ago for an assault upon Mrs. Murray Shields, and who was taken to Louisville for safe keeping.

ALLEGED LYNCHERS TRIED.
Rumors of Trouble, Which Is Prepared for, But Comes Not.
Lake City, Fla., Aug. 20.—The preliminary trial of John Walker, J. M. Rhodan, L. D. and W. B. Padgett and Thomas Phillips, white men, charged with lynching the negro preacher, Robert Bennett, on July 4, took place here to-day. There was little evidence against the accused and they were discharged.

About fifty white men, friends of the accused, came to town heavily armed, to see that the negroes did not attempt to harm them. So much excitement was caused by a rumor that a carload of armed negroes was coming from Jacksonville to lynch the prisoners that the mayor ordered all the saloons closed. There were many negroes in town, but they made no demonstration and the anticipated trouble did not materialize.

Preacher Bennett was lynched for an attempted assault on the little daughter of W. B. Padgett. Five hundred dollars reward has been offered by Gov. Mitchell for the arrest and conviction of the lynchers, but it is not thought the state will ever have to pay it.

THE LYNCHING BUSINESS.
A Ringing Article from the Race Published by Judge Tourgee.
After all that has been said, and in view of the facts themselves, how easily Northern people are fooled in regard to the real animus that under-lies the lynching of negroes in the South.

It is almost impossible to discuss this matter without being met with the remark. "Well of course I don't believe in lynching, but you can't blame people much for protecting the honor of their wives and daughters even by illegal means."

It never seems to occur to these people that in 19 cases out of 20, there is absolutely no proof forthcoming that Negroes who have been lynched as the reports allege, for foul crimes. In discussing a case of this kind with a shrewd business man, the writer was met by the statement "Why the brute himself confessed that he was guilty." "How do you know he confessed?" he was asked. "The paper said so." was the reply. Just think of this as evidence! A Negro is burned at the stake, some agent, perhaps himself one of the fiends who helped to do the deed, or a neighbor and a sympathizer with those who did, sends a press despatch that the man was caught by an armed mob, confessed the crime, and was then done to death. To whom did he confess? What did he confess? Under what circumstances? These details are too unimportant. The report does not say. It very likely depends on the word of some chivalrous gentleman who believes in burning a "nigger" at the stake, or in shooting him to death if he asks for his wages. Shall he be insulted by being asked to support his word by any evidence? Assuredly not.

But as to the probabilities (although one would hardly think it just in his own case to be convicted on probabilities,) is it probable that there are as many cases of rape and assaults as reported? To our mind it is, The Negro has so long been treated like a beast that it is wonder that some of the race degenerate to the level of the beasts, and then too, has been so long and so often ignored, why should he not cease to respect virtue and honor?

But tracing probabilities farther; if such crimes are frequently committed (and nothing ought to prove an excuse to prevent their most certain and terrible punishment,) then from all we can learn from the reports that are given in the press, and from those that come in more direct and circumstantial way, it is so probable as to be almost an absolute certainty, that it does not make any great difference what particular Negro suffers for the crime. Since there are no little formalities of trial or proof or even of investigation, one "nigger" will answer for a victim as well as another. Whether he be guilty or innocent, he will make a horrible example, and one "niggar" more or less is of small account.

If anyone doubts the justice or fairness of this statement or the case, let him read the press despatch of the latest reported case which is as follows:

At Hope Henry, in a colored church five miles west of Lake City, Fla., a party took Robert Bennett, a young colored preacher from the pulpit, carried him a short distance off, and lynched him. When the body was found by the roadside, the preacher and took him away. His offense, it is said, was an assault upon a white woman in Sewanee County recently, and from there the lynchers are said to have come. The usual warning was left attached to the body.

Notice the wording of the report. The man was taken in the night from among a crowd of sleeping Negroes. Considering the fact that he was being taken to his execution, the identification cannot be said to have been very careful. Again the report says, "His offense, it is said, was an assault upon a white woman in Sewanee County, recently." At the best, it is a mere report, a report of an assault upon a white woman. What woman? Oh, a woman. Where? In Sewanee County; the precise location is no matter, somewhere in the county. But when was this mysterious as-ault upon an impersonal someone, in an uncertain somewhere, for which a man is dragged from sleep among a crowd, in the night, to pay the penalty of his life.—in the name of justice, when was this offense committed? Why "recently" sometime this week or is year, when the need of being so circumstantial it name the day when it is only a "gagar" preacher that is to be murdered and mutilated. God pity the country where such crimes of this call forth protest here

VICTIMS OF MOB LAW.
One Hundred and Four People Murdered Since March Last.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN—Sir: The frequency with which acts of lawlessness on the part of mobs in all parts of the country are recorded in the daily newspapers has very materially blunted the public conscience into indifference to the gravity of the situation in this respect. The every-day report of mob violence does not appear to disturb the public conscience. It is taken and regarded as one of the stereotyped features of the news of the day. The murder of a citizen by his fellow citizens banded together as a mob does not apparently affect the general opinion of those whose business it is to create and control public opinion. And yet all law-abiding citizens admit that the orderly administration of the laws is the only safeguard that society has against demoralization, and that the only way to deal with criminals is by regular legal process.

It is only when the mob oversteps the bounds of humanity, as in the murder of the eleven Italians by the people of New Orleans, or the torturing and burning in a public square of a half-witted negro by the people of Paris, Texas, that the public conscience shows a disposition to resent the obtrusion of mobocracy as a central force in the government of society.

Crime thrives upon what it feeds. It proceeds from one excess to another by gradual stages, seeking always novelty in its methods. By gradual stages it progresses until a climax is reached beyond which it does not seem possible to go. The Paris incident was of this character. It was an incident for which there can be no apology or excuse.

The best men of the place justified it, however, upon grounds of public necessity, and abused everybody who did not accept their views of the situation. But there is no doubt in the minds of any one that the people of Paris who participated in that horrid crime will never recover from the degrading influence of it.

The New Orleans incident produced an international complication. Some Italians had been murdered in cold blood. They were in the hands of the law and legal authority. The evidence against them was sufficient to convict them or exonerate them. But the citizens of New Orleans, acting upon an impulse of madness, undertook to take the law of the State into their own hands, and in doing so violated a vital principle of international law and risked a war with a friendly power. This was averted only by the payment to the aggrieved of an indemnity, in the payment of which Louisiana had only an indirect part. It refused as a corporate body to give any satisfaction to the State Department at Washington or to the Italian Foreign Office. To preserve the good relations of the Federal Government to a friendly foreign power, the United States were compelled to pay the $20,000 demanded by justice. The whole people of the country were compelled to pay for the lawlessness of a single State.

In the August number of the Basis, Judge Albion W. Tourgee estimates the number of mob murders from March 1, 1895, to Aug. 1 to be 104. This is a fearful number of people to be slaughtered outside of the pale of the law. The crimes for which these people were murdered are entirely irrelevant as an excuse. Criminals are supposed to be innocent in the eye of the law until they are proven to be guilty as charged, and the verdict of no mob, however respectable the elements which compose it, can be taken as a sufficient warrant for its lawlessness. Judge Tourgee gives the following record for the month of July alone, and it is sufficient to shock the moral sense of Christian mankind:

Marshall E. Price, Denton, Md., July 2, hanged, colored, male; murder. Two, names unknown, Guthrie, O.T., July 2, nanged, white, males; horse stealing. John Barnwell, Edgefield, S. C., July 3, shot, colored, male, by four white boys; no excuse given. The Rev. Robert Bennett, Lake City, Fla., July 4, shot, colored; said to have attempted outrage on white woman. Theodore Puckett, Pelahatchie Creek, Miss., July 4, hanged, colored, male; charged with stealing money. Thomas Parker, Baldwin county, Miss., July 4, hanged, colored, male; charged with stealing watch. Joseph Howton, Princeton, Ky., July 4, shot, white, male; no excuse given. Howlet Howton, Princeton, Ky., July 4, shot, white, male; no excuse given. William Walker, New Orleans, La., July 9, white, male, shot by posse; said to be a desperado. Scot Vaughn, New Orleans, La., July 10, shot, colored, male; did not want ditch dug in front of his own house. Two men, names not known, Hampton, Ark., July 13, hanged, colored, males; accused of murder. Bob Haggard, Winchester, Ky., July 14, hanged, colored, m
riot at Brookside Mines, Ala. John Tinsley, Meridian, Miss., July 14, shot, colored, male; interfered to prevent colored woman being chastised. Mary Hunley, white, Cora Pace, colored, and Lewis Stewart, white, July 10, whipped; charged with adultery; taken out of jail, given 100 lashes, then returned to jail. Summary: Total, 37; total killed, 31; shot through shoulder, 1; whipped, 5; white, 6; colored, 31; hanged, 11; shot to death, 20; males, 32; females, 5.

The tendency to lynch law violence is constantly on the increase. That public sentiment in certain centres is largely against sustaining the officers of the law as against a mob is borne out by the Roanoke incident, where, after protecting his prisoner by firing into the mob, the military officer was compelled to flee from the place, as well as the Mayor. A similar condition of affairs recently developed in an Ohio town. Four men were recently lynched in California. There have been three lynchings in Ohio within the year, and one at least in Iowa. It is a very dull day in the South when some man is not swung up to a tree and riddled with bullets, charged with some alleged offence against law and order and decency, and who could more wisely and safely be turned over to the lawful authorities to be punished in the usual and proper way. The history of the Paris Commune teaches that the mob cannot be relied upon to do other than destroy life and property and to subvert government. The reign of the mob in the United States is gaining a firmer hold every year, and it behooves those who believe in law and order to face it resolutely and fight it down.

NEW YORK, Aug. 30. T. THOMAS FORTUNE.

EDINBURG ITEMS.
Mr. L. M. Hisey is improving his residence by painting and repairing it.
Mr. J. W. Santmiers and their daughter, Mrs. Gearing, have returned from a visit to friends in Clarke county.
Mr. Brown and family of Washington, and a number of others are boarding at Mrs. McGinnis.
Miss Mollie Whitmore has returned from a visit to friends in Rockingham county.
Miss Kate Osborn, of this place, after a visit to Miss Pearl Clinedinst returned home, last Monday.
Mrs. Coffman and daughter of Charles-town are visiting Mrs. P. J. Allison.
A little lady made her appearance at the home of Mr. Marcus Jack recently. She evidently intended to stay awhile.
Miss Cora Pumphrey, of Washington and Miss Lucy Hollingsworth, of River Side, spent several days last week with Mr. and Mrs. S. P. Hollingsworth.
Rev. Mr. Sampsell of the U. B. Church will preach at Willow Grove next Sunday, afternoon.
Mrs. Brawlie and daughter Miss Ruby are boarding at Mrs. Anna Grandstaff's. They are much pleased with our town and surroundings.
Mrs. P. J. Allison has been quite ill for some days.
Mrs. Ella Downey, of Mt. Jackson has been visiting Miss Lucy Downey, of this place.
The huckleberries still come in in large quantities.
Miss Belle Dunifee, of Penn., is visiting Dr. and Mrs. Hisey is improving his residence by painting and repairing it.
Messrs. T. J. Marston and Jacob Bowman are remodeling the bridge on the Fort road.

Mrs. Edward Whissen, of this place, is visiting Mrs. Fanny Dinges, at Middletown.

Miss Birdie Cooper returned home last week after a visit of some months in Ohio.

Mrs. H. A. Whissen and two children who have been quite sick are now improving.

Mr. Jas. Rau is improving the appearance of his residence.

The Mount Jackson base ball club came down last Tuesday to "flax" our boys, but went back with a score of 32 to 2 in favor of Edinburg. We treat them all alike.

A Woodstock coon who had been employed here for some weeks and had passed herself off as a widow, was ducked in Stony Creek on account of her misconduct and notified to leave the place within three days. She wisely took warning and left us. May she never come back.

Mrs. Proctor who lives with her two small children in this place, last week one night heard a noise in the room across the hall. She supposed it was something after the milk. On attempting to walk across the hall, she was grasped by a man, who had attempted to disguise himself by blacking his face and hands. She was severely choked, but the noise made by her efforts attracted the attention of this place a neighbor who hastened to her relief. The scounderl made his escape. In reply to your senile correspondent, "Spectator," to whom everything, except his own assertions, seem "puerile" or "school boy style" or "pleading the baby act," I have but a few words. His own language reminds us of the old adage, "once a man and twice a child." He prepares himself for defeat by giving an excuse in advance and saying, "it will be a victory of men over boys." It was a terrible crime, in his sight, for an Edinburg boy to question the decisions of a Woodstock umpire, and yet this very manly club called "The Kids," got their backs up, and sulked and broke up the game because they did not like the decisions of the umpire. We promised you "to flax" them, but even the influence of their old chief, Mr. Letcher Burner, could not keep them on the field long enough to receive the flaxing we had in store for them. But really, Mr. Spectator, don't you think that a club that can boast of college students and young men that escort ladies through the streets, is rather ancient to be called "Kids," and to cry "your men beat our boys!"

Don't you think another club "hurt their reputation as ball-players," and that a club nearer home should heed your overkind advice?
